intro: Based on your answers, here is how your team ships, what that is likely costing you, and what we would do about it first.

industryNotes.adtech: In AdTech the hard part is usually the reporting surface. Every stakeholder wants a different cut of the same data, so dashboards accumulate columns and filters until the people actually running campaigns go build their own spreadsheets. It is also worth being honest about which product you are building: the buyer-facing surface and the internal ops tooling have different users and different standards, and teams that treat them as one product tend to underserve both.
industryNotes.enterprise-saas: In enterprise SaaS the cost of a confusing product lands on your own team first, as onboarding time and support load, and on renewals after that. The split that matters most is admin versus end user. The person who buys and configures your product is almost never the person living in it daily, and a product designed around the admin's mental model tends to stall at expansion, because the people who would drive that expansion never got comfortable.
industryNotes.fintech: In fintech the UX problem is a trust problem. Users need to understand what is about to happen before it happens, and the cost of a misunderstood action is higher than almost anywhere else, because money moves and it is hard to unwind. Compliance constrains what you can change and how quickly, which makes it tempting to treat the interface as fixed. It usually is not: most of what makes these products hard to use is habit rather than regulation.
industryNotes.other: Whatever the vertical, the pattern holds. The gap between how your team understands the product and how a new user encounters it is where rework comes from. The teams that close that gap fastest are not the ones with the biggest research budget — they are the ones watching real users often enough that it never gets wide.

offerings.design-system-embedded: A design system gives your team a set of decisions that are already made, so the same questions stop coming back every sprint. We build it against your real product rather than in the abstract, and we embed with your team while it lands, because a system nobody adopts is just a component library. We did this for Metacloud, a premium OpenStack product, where one component library ended up carrying the customer dashboard, the self-serve support portal, and the internal tools their own operations team worked in.
offerings.ux-audit-product-design: We start with an audit: where new users stall, what they misunderstand, and which screens are generating your support tickets. Then we redesign the paths that matter, in priority order, so the improvement shows up in onboarding time rather than in a deck. We did this for ReachEdge, a lead-management product used by more than 3,000 small businesses, where the redesign began by surfacing core functions that navigation had buried.
offerings.strategy-prototyping: When a team cannot agree on what to build, the fastest way through is usually something concrete to react to. We run product strategy in parallel with rapid prototyping, so the arguments happen against an artifact and the decision closes in weeks instead of quarters. We did this after ReachLocal was acquired by Gannett and two merged sales organizations needed a single way to put a proposal in front of a prospect. Both sides agreed on scope before any pixels moved, and the argument was settled against a working proof of concept.
offerings.design-system: We build the system your teams are already improvising: components, patterns, and the rules for which to use when. The work is as much about adoption as about the library — documentation, a contribution model, and whatever it takes for the fifth team to pick it up as readily as the first. We did this for tvScientific, where one system carries the reporting, data visualization, and campaign tools of a connected-TV advertising platform.
offerings.research-measurement: We set up the measurement first: what you expect to change, how you will know, and what the baseline is. Then research runs against it continuously rather than as a one-time study, so your team can point at the difference a release made instead of arguing about it. We did this for Start It Up, whose platform evaluates entrepreneurs for government accelerator programs: research and stakeholder interviews shaped what got built, rather than explaining it afterward.

assumptions: This is an estimate, not an audit. It applies the rework share you reported to the team size you reported, at a fully loaded cost per person. The useful part is the order of magnitude. If the number looks wrong, the interesting question is which assumption you would change.
unmeasuredNote: You told us you are not sure how much time goes to rework, so this figure assumes 10%, which is on the low side of what we usually see. That uncertainty is worth acting on by itself: teams who cannot answer this question generally cannot tell whether anything they try is working. Measuring it for one quarter is the cheapest move on this list.
